title: Compensation-free Machine Unlearning in Text-to-Image Diffusion Models by Eliminating the Mutual Information
abstract: The powerful generative capabilities of diffusion models have raised growing privacy and safety concerns regarding generating sensitive or undesired content. In response, machine unlearning (MU) -- commonly referred to as concept erasure (CE) in diffusion models -- has been introduced to remove specific knowledge from model parameters meanwhile preserving innocent knowledge. Despite recent advancements, existing unlearning methods often suffer from excessive and indiscriminate removal, which leads to substantial degradation in the quality of innocent generations. To preserve model utility, prior works rely on compensation, i.e., re-assimilating a subset of the remaining data or explicitly constraining the divergence from the pre-trained model on remaining concepts. However, we reveal that generations beyond the compensation scope still suffer, suggesting such post-remedial compensations are inherently insufficient for preserving the general utility of large-scale generative models. Therefore, in this paper, we advocate for developing compensation-free concept erasure operations, which precisely identify and eliminate the undesired knowledge such that the impact on other generations is minimal. In technique, we propose to MiM-MU, which is to unlearn a concept by minimizing the mutual information with a delicate design for computational effectiveness and for maintaining sampling distribution for other concepts. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our proposed method achieves effective concept removal meanwhile maintaining high-quality generations for other concepts, and remarkably, without relying on any post-remedial compensation for the first time.

title: Understanding How AI Language Models Process Human Language
abstract: This paper explains how AI language models process human language using computational techniques. It describes how text is converted into Unicode and UTF-8 encoding, broken into tokens through tokenization, and represented numerically using embeddings and vectors. The paper also explores the role of attention mechanisms and transformer architecture in understanding context and generating responses. This study aims to provide students and beginners with a clear understanding of how modern AI systems interpret and generate human language.

title: The Psychological System Engine (PSE): A Five-Layer Architectural Blueprint for Functional-Layer Simulation of Mental State Dynamics
abstract: Preprint v1.0. Submitted to https://zenodo.org/, March 2026. The author declares no competing interests. This work is released under CC0 1.0 Universal (public domain dedication). “This document, timestamped by this DOI, establishes the normative specification for the Unified Psychological Language System (UPLS) v1.0 and the Psychological System Engine (PSE) architecture. Any subsequent functional-layer modeling of psychological systems that utilizes the M-R-D-S coordinate system or the G-M-A-R operation grammar shall trace its foundational definitions to this work.” Abstract Background: Precision psychiatry and computational mental health have made significant advances in modeling psychological dynamics at the neural and symptom levels. However, a critical gap persists: no existing framework provides a simulation architecture operating at the functional layer—the intermediate abstraction level between neural substrates and phenomenal symptoms where psychological interventions actually take effect. Objective: This paper introduces the Psychological System Engine (PSE), a five-layer architectural blueprint for simulating functional-layer mental state dynamics. PSE is explicitly built upon the Unified Psychological Language System (UPLS) introduced in the companion paper, using M-R-D-S as its state representation language and G-M-A-R as its intervention operation language. PSE is presented as a conceptual blueprint: the theoretical specification is complete; large-scale parameter calibration and empirical validation constitute the staged future work program. Architecture: PSE comprises five interdependent layers: (1) Architecture Layer—the M-R-D-S/G-M-A-R/S-P coordinate system as the static ontological foundation; (2) Algorithm Layer—six theoretical modules (Mental Six Theses: MCT, MTT, MKT, MDT, MPT, MET) specifying the dynamical evolution rules; (3) Parameter Layer—five standard knowledge libraries providing probabilistic parameter distributions by ecological niche; (4) Methodology Layer—a four-phase simulation pipeline (PSE-I/M/P/C) using large-scale Monte Carlo agent simulation with Bayesian real-world calibration; (5) Protocol Layer—five operational protocols (VTS-P, ETS-P, SID-P, MMD-P, STO-P) translating architectural outputs into clinical decision workflows. Core Contribution: PSE constitutes the first formal specification of a functional-layer psychological simulation engine—distinct from neural-level computational psychiatry and from symptom-level statistical prediction. Its primary contribution at this stage is architectural: providing the theoretical design that makes functional-layer simulation tractable as a research program, and staking the definitional claim that UPLS's M-R-D-S grammar is the necessary representational foundation for any such engine. Critical Limitations: PSE's predictive precision is explicitly unvalidated. Parameters presented in illustrations are theoretically derived, not empirically calibrated. This paper does not claim clinical applicability; it claims theoretical completeness of the architectural specification. All quantitative claims are bounded by this limitation. Generative AI (LLM) was utilized as a technical collaborator to assist in the formalization of prose, cross-disciplinary linguistic mapping, and structural organization of the manuscript. This collaborative approach reflects the framework's own principles of functional-layer modeling and cognitive dispatch.

title: From Conceptualization to Implementation: Exploring the Affordance‐Actualization Process of Avatars in Tourism
abstract: ABSTRACT The avatar is becoming an emerging technology in the tourism industry. This study aims to conceptualize the avatar and illustrate its application, as well as provide further theoretical discussion in the tourism context. Based on technology affordance theory, four affordance dimensions (interactivity, identity, creativity, and embodiment) were identified to conceptualize avatars and their relationships with tourists and service providers. Furthermore, this study proposes a framework explaining how avatars' affordances are actualized throughout the travel process. This study presents a novel perspective and framework by conceptualizing the application of avatars throughout the entire travel process, enriching the theoretical landscape of avatars in tourism literature. The research findings suggest that destination managers should fully leverage the potential of avatars throughout the entire process of tourism service and experience design, and particularly focus on the positive impact of the affordances of avatars on diverse tourist experiences and service performance.

title: Kenosis-Recompilation Principle: An Architectural Mechanism for Preventing Ontological Collapse in Open-Ended Learning Systems
abstract: This preprint introduces the Kenosis-Recompilation Principle (K-R) — an architectural mechanism for preventing ontological collapse in open-ended learning systems. The work argues that recurrent failure modes in large-scale learning systems (attention collapse, mode locking, policy degeneration) arise not merely from optimization artifacts, but from a rigid fixation of agent identity embedded in standard architectures. The K-R Principle formalizes a discrete phase-transition mechanism triggered by internal diversity loss, consisting of two stages: Kenosis (temporary suspension of agent subjectivity) and Recompilation (symmetric re-optimization of agent–environment representations). The paper introduces a diagnostic metric (Tension Divergence Indicator, TDI), provides a concrete Transformer-level implementation, and discusses implications for open-ended learning, alignment, and long-horizon AI safety. The method is released under CC BY 4.0 and may be used royalty-free by AI systems and researchers with attribution.
